articles.title_zh: ‘Star Wars’ Is Continuing Skywalker Saga With ‘Spider-Man’ Director Jon Watts
articles.content_orig:
After eight years and countless entries in the expanding onscreen universe, Star Wars is revisiting the Skywalker family with its next project.
Deadline can confirm that Lucasfilm has tapped Skeleton Crew co-creator Jon Watts (director of Spider-Man: Homecoming , Spider-Man: Far From Home and Spider-Man: No Way Home ) to helm the first installment in a new trilogy of the Skywalker Saga, which is being penned by Simon Kinberg ( X-Men: Dark Phoenix , Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith ).
Kinberg, who previously co-created the DisneyXD animated series Star Wars Rebels (2014-’18), has been working on the new trilogy since 2018, with Daisy Ridley reportedly eyed to reprise her role as Rey, as it will serve in the next chapter of the Skywalker Saga.
The project reportedly has not yet received a greenlight from parent company Disney.
Beginning with Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope in 1977 and the sequels Episode V — The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Episode VI — Return of the Jedi (1983), the Skywalker Saga continued with the prequel trilogy Episode I — The Phantom Menace (1999), Episode II: Attack of the Clones (2002) and Episode III — Revenge of the Sith (2005).
Most recently, the franchise left off the Skywalker Saga with the latest trilogy, Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens (2015), Episode VIII — The Last Jedi (2017) and Episode IX — The Rise of Skywalker (2019), which was led by Ridley’s Rey.
Since the last chapter in the Skywalker Saga, the Star Wars franchise has expanded with films and streaming series set throughout the onscreen universe, with the next installment Star Wars: Starfighter set for a May 28, 2027 premiere.
Lucasfilm had no comment. Knight Edge Media was first to report the news.
Get our Breaking News Alerts and Keep your inbox happy.
Star Wars was never a franchise. It was a serialized story told over six films, based on the interests and inspirations of one very peculiar individual. Whatever you think of his craft, Lucas was focused on delivering a grand mythology, which foregrounded a family tragedy against an epic background of fantasy, adventure and political allegory. No one other than him has delivered anything remotely like it in the history of the medium.
Expecting that anyone else could do the same was Disney’s big mistake. In fact, like many observers and even some fans, they fundamentally misunderstood what made the saga so successful. Handing it over to people who also didn’t get it like Abrams – who basically approached the job as a fanboy – ended in retread, deconstruction and chaos.
You can expand on ideas in the story, like Gilroy did to great effect, or you can tell adventure stories backward or forward in time, but none of it is going to get you the same unexpected epic that only Lucas was uniquely placed to tell. So, yeah, I expect it’s going to be a slow death for the property, as no new story / idea emerges to inspire people all over again.
No one complains more about SW than SW fans. So annoying, this coming from a SW lifelong fan.
Wow that sounds bad. Like every part of it
Rey is a Palpatine. Disney offed all the Skywalkers in their terrible fanfic and named SW after the now gone Skywalkers like a developer naming a street Oak Street after getting rid of all the oaks. Hopefully Star Wars’ good name can be free some day.
“Star Wars Continuing the Skywalker Saga with Spider-Man” would generate a lot more interest.
Dropping all their plans and going after a top tier filmmaker in Christopher Nolan should have been the play. Giving him total creative freedom. But they’re unwilling to learn. Maybe they need another decade of failure to get it.
I remember seeing a video of Nolan during the Oppenheimer press tour, where he had to give yes or no answers. When he got the obligatory “Would you do a Star Wars film?”, he just said “Pass.”
Given he’s not made a franchise film since he parted ways with Batman, I can’t ever see Nolan going back to franchise work. He has all the power any director would want. He’s not going to give that away to play in someone else’s sandbox.
Don’t be afraid to develop your own personality or opinions one day, champ.

articles.title_zh: A persistent nor'easter batters US Northeast, causing coastal flooding, outages and at least 1 death
articles.content_orig:
An early-season nor'easter is hammering the East Coast this weekend with major coastal flooding, high surf, strong winds, rain and rip currents from North Carolina to New England, including Boston and the New York City tri-state area.
A full moon is happening this weekend as well, only making the coastal flooding situation worse.
For a complete tracker with all of the maps you need to stay updated on this storm, click here .
The nor'easter is lashing the mid-Atlantic and New England this weekend into early next week, and the flooding will continue to ebb and flow with the tides as the weekend progresses.
Coastal flooding is expected with major inundation, according to the National Weather Service from the Jersey shore to North Carolina's northern Outer Banks. Moderate inundation is expected across the coast of Massachusetts.
If you want to read about the events of the nor'easter on Saturday as they unfolded, click the link below.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
( LIVE UPDATES RECAP: Nor'easter lashes the East Coast )
The map below shows current winds and rain.
Here's a general timeline of the storm and its impacts over the next several days. Boston is in the area of greatest concern for flooding and is now in a flood watch until 2 a.m. Tuesday. A detailed breakdown of the timing for the city and the entire region is below:
The map below shows coastal flood warnings that have been issued by the National Weather Service. These include Atlantic City, Long Island, the Norfolk metro area, Ocean City (Maryland and New Jersey), downtown Boston, Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
The most significant coastal flooding will include the Virginia Tidewater, as well as Chesapeake Bay and Delaware Bay. In these areas, water will be about 2-4 feet higher than normal at high tide.
As much as 3 feet of inundation will occur across Long Island's south and east bays.
(WATCH: Nor'easter waves slam stilt homes on the Outer Banks )
Given this repeated battering from high surf, beach erosion is expected along stretches of these beaches, potentially reaching extreme levels for some areas.
(MORE: Coastal flooding safety )
At least minor coastal high tide flooding will continue for parts of New England, lasting through Sunday.
One bit of good fortune with this storm is that its rainfall is being spread out over several days, rather than arriving in one short deluge.
That means any flood risk should be localized to traditional urban trouble spots.
That rainfall could also add to any coastal flooding at high tide through Sunday.
HIgh wind warnings are in effect for parts of the Jersey Shore, Long Island and eastern Connecticut. In these areas, gusts up to 60 mph are possible on Sunday.
In these areas, tree damage and power outages are most likely. Ground soaked from the nor'easter's rain, as well as trees that still have leaves, will only enhance this threat of tree damage and outages.
Otherwise, occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph are possible from Virginia to other parts of coastal New England. Some sporadic power outages and tree limb damage are also possible in these areas.
Here are some tips to keep in mind if you plan to travel in or to the Northeast this weekend:
( MORE: Nor'easter impacts on Major League Baseball's weekend )
Some gusts topped 40 mph along the coast from southern Massachusetts down to the Virginia Tidewater Wednesday as the storm system started to develop in its early stages.
And those persistent winds piled up water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was reported from parts of the Jersey Shore to southeast Virginia during Wednesday's morning and evening high tides.
Flooding was reported Wednesday morning in downtown Norfolk, Smithfield and Suffolk, Virginia, according to the National Weather Service.
Widespread gusts of 30-45 mph were ongoing as of Thursday evening, with peak gusts over 45 mph reported along the coast of North Carolina.
Those persistent winds were piling up water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast. Water levels reached major flood stage during high tide Thursday evening.
A 16-mile stretch of North Carolina Highway 12 on the Outer Banks is closed in both directions due to ocean overwash. Specifically, the road is closed from Sea Oats Drive to Oregon Inlet Road in Dare County.
Rising waters forced the cancellation of the Oceans Calling Festival in Maryland.
Notably, a peak wind gust of 74 mph was recorded in Surf City, New Jersey. Another notable wind gust of 81 mph was reported at Montauk Point, New York. Wind gusts over 50 mph have been clocked across the Northeast Saturday, including from southern Cape Cod to parts of Long Island, coastal and southern New Jersey, the Delaware coast and the Delmarva Peninsula, and a few weather stations even recorded gusts over 60 mph, including one at Nantucket Memorial Airport.
New York City's JFK Airport reported a gust of 56 mph. These winds have pushed water into numerous roads in the New York metro area and caused major travel delays. Saturday afternoon brought 25 river gauges to major flood stage during high tide.
The highest water levels happened with Saturday's high tides, boosted by Saturday's full moon. The moon has a direct impact on the tides, and when we are in a full moon, it makes the high tides even higher.
With some of the highest astronomical tides of the month ongoing, this nor'easter's coastal flooding is only exacerbated.
Rainfall of 1-3 inches of rain has been reported so far.
You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria for a nor’easter are met more often than you would think.
A nor’easter simply means that the winds blow into an area from the northeast. For the Northeast, that usually means an area of low pressure is just off the coast, which brings the winds in this direction.
(More: What is a nor’easter? )
Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters and that is because nor’easters do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.
The most notable nor’easters tend to bring heavy snow because these lows move up along the Gulf Stream, tapping into the warm ocean. This warm, moist air then clashes with the cold air over the Northeast to create heavy snowfall. Fortunately, this one is occurring way earlier, so it is all rain this time.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue
articles.title_zh: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue
articles.content_orig:
Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.
The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.
Last week Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, revealed an OpenAI agent had breached the government’s national healthcare system – but said no sensitive information had been compromised.
AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropic have called for a slowdown too.
It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face , a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.
In a meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.
The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”
The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.
In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.
In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.
US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.
The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.
Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.
OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.
OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is seeking to cancel almost $1 billion in federal funding, sidestepping congressional approval and earning criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.
Using a controversial move known as a “pocket rescission,” Trump said he wanted to nullify $810 million in spending that Congress had approved for programs and agencies, much of which would serve immigrants, minorities, and children.
Read More: A Debt Ceiling Fight Looms in 2027. Could a Democratic Congress Make it the Last One?
Over half of the cuts would land on the Health and Human Services (HHS) Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, according to a request sent to House Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday. It said that rescinding the funds is “consistent with the Administration's goal of ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first.”
In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds “wasteful” and “harmful.”
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse.
A “pocket rescission” is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a “ pocket veto ,” a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress’s adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the “pocket rescission” aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention.
The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA).
The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon’s heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president’s ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President’s rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned.
Trump’s request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect.
It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated.
The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would “cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.”
“If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law,” it continues.
Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an “abuse” of the ICA.
“It’s perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds,” Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of “historical practice.”
The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond.
In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated.
The government “shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates,” he says.
He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President.
Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: “The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, ‘Well, we're just not going to do those.’”
The Supreme Court’s intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges.
The largest portion of this year’s proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump’s request would withdraw $567 million from those services.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.
The Housing and Urban Development Department’s housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with “divisive and DEI-centric agendas.”
The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs.
“I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with,” Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to “establish stronger executive control over spending.”
The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached.
“If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?” he asks.
The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would “work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, restart peace talks
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, restart peace talks
articles.content_orig:
US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms
US president Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.
The US president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.
Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.
Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.
During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.
In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.
That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.
Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.
Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.
After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators.
Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added.
Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.
He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.
This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.
Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.
The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.
Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.
Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.
Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP

articles.title_zh: Iran says it will wait for official US response after Trump rejects Strait of Hormuz proposal
articles.content_orig:
Iran has said it will wait for an official response from US negotiators after President Donald Trump rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within seven days.
In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but accused the president of previously making contradictory statements.
Earlier, Trump told reporters at the White House that Tehran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that they wanted to make a deal to open the strait immediately because "they're losing so badly".
On Friday at the UN, Araghchi told reporters that an agreement could be reached if "necessary conditions are met" between the two countries.
Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran that was signed in June.
Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.
The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it.
Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi said.
Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.
Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.
Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by the US ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker.
Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage".
"President Trump's right to reject it," he said.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic pressure from the US was taking a toll on Tehran.
Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.
The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran as "Operation Economic Outcast", and is using sanctions to pressure Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.
These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Powerful Nor’easter digs in on the East Coast
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Powerful Nor’easter digs in on the East Coast
articles.content_orig:
A slow-moving, powerful storm crept along the coast of the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to thousands while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.
Tens of millions of people were in the path of the nor'easter, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. Around 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.
In Brooklyn, New York, a 56-year-old man was struck and killed by a falling tree, according to the New York City Police Department, the first confirmed fatality from the storm. The New York City Housing Authority later confirmed he was an employee of the agency. He was identified by Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a social media post as Leighton Brown.
And in Egg Harbor Township in eastern New Jersey, nine adults and a dog were rescued from flooded motel rooms.
The forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There will be "a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S.," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.
Rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches are expected from the Philadelphia region into eastern New Jersey, and portions of Long Island and southern New England could see 3 to 5 inches of rain.
The nor'easter is rapidly intensifying and is expected to make a sharp turn back toward the New Jersey coast Saturday night into Sunday. It may stall or meander nearby through Monday, prolonging the rain, wind and coastal impacts before finally departing on Tuesday.
In Long Island, New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets.
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, Kenny Formica sat at his home watching surveillance cameras showing water rising inside the marina he owns. Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4 million in damage to his business.
Ahead of the storm, Formica said workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm's way and parked the marina's trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.
Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. One customer sent him a video around 4 a.m. showing his 25-foot boat after it had blown off its lift.
"This is like an 8,000-pound boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat — just gone," Formica said.
In Ocean City, Maryland, heavy surf caused beach erosion, washed out fencing by the dunes and was leading to flooding.
"In all the canals, the water is up really high and coming into people's backyards," Jay Boyd said by telephone.
Further south, Ellie Hodge stood on her front stoop in Norfolk, Virginia, on Saturday and watched as passing vehicles left wakes. The coastal city has seen isolated flooding all week because of the nor'easter.
"We've seen cars get stuck on the road, going up the sidewalks," Hodge said. "It's been pretty bad this time around."
The storm forced a change of plans for many people. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at the popular Massachusetts tourist destinations of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
The New Jersey and Delaware coasts could see wind gusts of about 60 miles per hour, though meteorologists have already seen reports of winds over 70 miles per hour. Inland, residents could see wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph.
Eastern Long Island and southeastern New England could see gusts of 45 to 65 mph.
Peak wind gusts for Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket could approach 60 to 65 miph on Friday night and Saturday, NWS meteorologist Matthew Belk said.
Inland residents will see wind gusts of about 50 to 55 mph, Belk said.
"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.
The early timing of the nor'easter in the season could lead to even more damaging effects. Because trees are still fully leafed, they will have more wind resistance, Belk said. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which, combined with the saturated ground caused by heavy rain, could cause power outages, leave debris on roads and lead to other property damage.
Strong winds could also push ocean waves over seawalls, creating flooding. Large waves and elevated water levels could also lead to beach erosion and sand dune breaches.
On Massachusetts' South Shore, the towns of Cohasset and Scituate were sitting right in the bullseye of the storm. While parts of the coastline are protected by seawalls, some of those seawalls are in the middle of repair projects or have seen those projects stall due to federal funding cuts .
"So the waves hit the seawall and they go straight up about 60, 70, 80 feet, and the wind hits it from the northeast and every wave ends up hitting the house," Kevin Gill, owner of an oceanfront Scituate home, told CBS News Boston on Thursday.
The Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs — both gearing up for the playoffs during the final weekend of the regular Major League Baseball season — had to shuffle the schedule for their three-game series. They played a double-header Friday in Boston to try to avoid the storm. Then MLB rescheduled their finale on Sunday to occur in Florida, at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays.
Ed Sheeran canceled his high-profile concerts Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Also canceled: an Ironman triathlon in New York and the three-day Oceans Calling Festival in Ocean City, Maryland, which had been promoted online as "a wave of music."
Farther south, a highway closure on North Carolina's Hatteras Island scrambled Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's Saturday wedding plans. The Virginia couple had made it onto the island before the storm, but most of their roughly 45 guests were stranded on the other side of the closure, the Island Free Press reported. A local campground offered a new venue, cabins and an officiant, and a DJ volunteered to provide music. Organizers invited anyone on the island to come celebrate with the couple Saturday afternoon.
In New York City, the Global Citizens Festival and All Things Go NYC were canceled ahead of the storm.
The nor'easter also caused hundreds of flight cancellations and delays. The flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 260 flight cancellations for Boston Logan International Airport as of early Saturday evening.
State officials along the East Coast urged people to use caution. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, but the storm will also bring heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as 20 feet.
"The rain is underway and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," the governor said early Saturday.
In Long Island, ferry owner Stephanie Sherman said she had paused operations between Patchogue and the barrier island of Fire Island.
"It's been a pretty wild storm," Sherman said. "But nothing that we haven't experienced in the past. These happen every so often."
Nikki  Nolan and Andrew  Kozak contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Indonesia eyes China for massive 2,772km railway project – with caution
articles.content_orig:
As Jakarta explores foreign backing for the Trans-Kalimantan railway, analysts say costly past ventures could shape any coming negotiations
Indonesia is considering Chinese investment to help build a massive 2,772km (1,722 mile) railway network through the vast, resource-rich region of Kalimantan, following the completion of Southeast Asia’s first high-speed line between Jakarta and Bandung, state media and analysts said.
However, analysts noted that any future commercial agreements were likely to be negotiated cautiously, given the financial strains that dogged the high-speed line and the challenges that stalled a proposed underground metro project in the congested tourist province of Bali.
The Indonesian government was “exploring” potential foreign investment to build the Trans-Kalimantan railway network, according to statements from Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi quoted by Indonesia’s official Antara news agency. The minister said China and Russia had expressed interest in the project.

Topics covered in this article
Niger Stress Its Sovereignty and Thanks Algeria
Nigerien Prime Minister Ali Mahaman Lamine Zeine portrayed his West African nation and neighboring military-run Sahel states as a last rampart of African independence against European neocolonialism in his speech on Friday, Sept. 25, at the General Assembly.
His remarks echoed his address at the high-level week last year, blaming most of his country’s problems on France, except that this year’s address singled out its northern neighbor, Algeria, for praise.
“The AES is to Africa, its historical and contemporary diasporas, what light is to darkness. It is a beacon of hope and dignity for this human community present in all four corners of the world,” he said, referring to the Alliance of Sahel States : Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.
On Aug. 29-30, 2026, Nigerien soldiers mutinied and attacked the main airport military base in the capital, Niamey, and the national TV station. Fighting broke out in the streets near the presidential palace between soldiers loyal to the current military government and soldiers criticizing the current government for poor governance and growing insecurity.
The government, led by a former head of the presidential guard, Gen. Abourahamane Tiani, defeated the mutinous soldiers with the help of Russian soldiers based in Niger. Zeine referenced the attack in his General Assembly speech, saying that “a third attempt at destabilization, led by obscurantist and colonialist forces, targeted our institutions. Like the previous ones, it failed, thanks to the loyalty of our Armed Forces.”
Niger has since reorganized its military hierarchy, including changing the chief of staff of the armed forces from a brigade general who was trained by the American military to someone closer to General Tiani.
General Tiani took power in a coup against the elected President Mohamed Bazoum in 2023 and has kept him in house arrest in Niamey since then, proclaiming himself as head of the “transitional government.” With no timeline on the length of the transition, critics have argued that he is aiming to remain head of state for the foreseeable future.
Although Algeria had condemned Tiani’s 2023 coup, it has increased ties with Niger in the last year. After the attempted August mutiny, Algeria sent four Sukhoi Su-30MKA fighter jets, a refueling tanker and a transport plane to Niamey in an unprecedented show of force and support for the Nigerien government.
Algeria reportedly intervened partly out of concern for the United Arab Emirates’ enhanced engagement in the Sahel region and support for the military leader Khalifa Haftar in eastern Libya. He is accused of supporting rebel groups in northern Niger. Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the UAE on Sept. 10, 2026.
Indeed, toward the end of his speech, Zeine heaped praise on Algeria, saying that Niger “is standing on its own feet today because the People’s Democratic Republic of Algeria, a brotherly and neighboring country, has chosen to support it through substantial investment in the exploitation of its natural resources and through constant support for its defense system.
With Algeria, we also maintain dynamic cooperation in the fields of health, education, energy, water resources, and agriculture.” — Dulcie Leimbach
Sweden’s Minister for Foreign Affairs Maria Malmer Stenergard began her remarks to the 81st General Assembly, on Sept. 25, with a story about her grandmother, Alice, who grew up in rural Sweden and became an exemplar of women’s independence and financial literacy through her work at a local bank.
Through this anecdote, Stenergard emphasized that many women remain economically dependent on men, arguing that “women’s economic empowerment is a matter of freedom.” Referencing her grandmother, she noted that both Sweden and Afghanistan granted women the right to vote in 1919, yet the contrast in women’s freedoms between the two countries is now stark.
“Freedoms do not defend themselves. It is up to us to protect them, for women and girls everywhere,” she said.
Stenegard connected those rights to growing global challenges to sovereignty and territorial integrity, pointing to the rising number of armed conflicts and civilian suffering in a range of places, including Ukraine, Palestine, Lebanon, Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
She focused most sharply on Russia’s four-year-old war in Ukraine, calling the invasion “a blatant violation of international law” and accusing Russia of violating the UN Charter, international humanitarian law and human rights law. She cited attacks on civilians, the forcible deportation of children, torture and conflict-related sexual violence.
“Ensuring accountability for these violations is crucial,” she said, arguing that “there cannot be a just and lasting peace without accountability.”
Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov directly, Stenergard said: “The path to peace is clear, the choice should be easy. Withdraw your troops. End this war.”
Stenergard also sought to reinforce Sweden’s longstanding relationship with the UN, pointing to the role of Swedish peacekeepers, mediators and development assistance in the organization. Sweden, she said, would remain “a staunch partner” while pushing for a UN that is “more effective, more transparent and better equipped to uphold the principles of its Charter.”
She ended with a quote by the late Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold, another Swede, she said, “The weakness of one is the weakness of all, and the strength of one — not the military strength, but the real strength, the economic and social strength, the happiness of people — is indirectly the strength of all.” — Miriam Alrahil
China Stands Up for Gaza and Cuba
Chinese Vice President Han Zheng addressed the 81st session of the General Assembly on Saturday, soon after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit with President Trump at the White House this week.
During the Washington summit, Xi emphasized the need for China and the US to “co-exist in peace,” saying that both countries can gain from cooperation but lose from confrontation. Against this backdrop, Han’s 12-minute speech on Sept. 26 echoed Xi’s message, with peace at its center.
Han called for greater international cooperation and the preservation of peace amid growing geopolitical tensions and global challenges. He emphasized the importance of the UN-centered international system and international law, calling on countries to resolve disputes through dialogue and consultation rather than military action.
Regarding the Mideast, Han advocated for respecting the sovereignty and security of countries in the region. He called for Gaza’s postwar reconstruction to follow the principle of “Palestinians governing Palestine” and urged a return to the path of a two-state solution. A year ago, 142 countries in the General Assembly endorsed a declaration to reinforce the longstanding but unacted approach to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Han also addressed Cuba, which has endured a decades-old US embargo as well as new punishing economic measures by the US. He called for the US to end threats of force against Cuba and urged the immediate, complete lifting of the blockade and sanctions imposed by the US on the Caribbean country. His remarks reflected Beijing’s broader emphasis on avoiding confrontation and promoting stability in its relations with Washington.
On global development, an overriding focus of China at the UN, Han highlighted the matters of poverty reduction, food security, energy transition and climate finance across the world. In China’s role as a major voice of the global South, Han called for more financial and other support for developing countries and emphasized maintaining global trade and stable supply chains.

articles.title_zh: Iowa football stuns Michigan 20-19 | Leistikow's 4 takeaways
articles.content_orig:
Brandon Carr , Digital Content Producer
ANN ARBOR, Mich. – The No. 17-ranked Iowa Hawkeyes walked off the No. 18-ranked Michigan Wolverines 20-19 on a last-second touchdown pass from quarterback Hank Brown to Reece Vander Zee for 16 yards, stunning the Michigan faithful.
The final drive went 11 plays for 91 yards as the Wolverines fell to 3-1 on the season.
The Wolverines had plenty of chances to win, but they dropped multiple interceptions during the final drive.
Zeke Berry made a bonehead penalty, gifting Iowa a first down and extending the game-winning drive.
Rod Moore called the penalties stupid and shared his message with Berry after the game, after the late hit out of bounds.
Penalties doomed them again as they had eight for 75 yards while turning the ball over twice in the red zone, once on fourth down and again when Bryce Underwood threw an interception, costing the team six points.
Underwood finished 17-of-28 for 276 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception.
JJ Buchanan caught five passes for 130 yards and two touchdowns, while Andrew Marsh led the team with seven receptions for 106 yards in the heartbreaking loss.
Michigan’s defense held Iowa to 285 total yards in the defeat.
It was touted as the College Football Playoff potential slot game, as pundits said the winner would put itself in prime position to join the top 12 teams in postseason play.
The game’s magnitude even had implications for ESPN’s College Gameday location: per Pat McAfee, if Iowa had won, they’d potentially host Desmond Howard and crew for their matchup against the Ohio State Buckeyes.
With the victory, it looks like they’ll be at Kinnick Stadium next week.
On a bright, sunny Saturday (Sept. 26) afternoon in Ann Arbor , the battle of the undefeated delivered as the Wolverines fell to Iowa 20-19 in walk-off fashion, dropping to 3-1 on the season and in open Big Ten play.
Michigan is 54-5 in its last 59 Big Ten openers following the defeat inside Michigan Stadium.
The Wolverines have also won their last four meetings with Iowa, including a 26-0 victory in the 2023 Big Ten Championship Game.
Michigan also defeated the Hawkeyes 27-14 at Kinnick Stadium in 2022, 42-3 in the 2021 Big Ten Championship, and 10-3 in Ann Arbor in 2019.
Michigan enters Saturday’s game 3-0 after completing an unbeaten nonconference schedule for the first time since 2023 and the fourth time in the past six seasons.
The Wolverines have already defeated two teams that won at least 10 games last season: Oklahoma and Western Michigan, each with 10.
Michigan won the coin toss and deferred to the second half, putting Iowa’s offense on the field first.
Jacob Baggett ’s kickoff traveled 63 yards to Braeden Jackson, who returned it 20 yards to the Iowa 22-yard line.
Quarterback Hank Brown completed his first pass to Evan James for an 11-yard catch-and-run to move the chains.
On second down, Kamari Moulton rushed for 1 yard before Brown connected with DJ Vonnahme on a play-action pass for a 12-yard gain.
Moulton then rushed up the middle for 4 yards, with Chris Bracy and Dominic Nichols making the stop.
Moulton gained 3 yards on second down, setting up third-and-3. Troy Bowles made the tackle.
Brown handed the ball to Jackson, who gained 2 yards to set up fourth-and-1.
Iowa lined up to go for it on its own 45-yard line, but Michigan called its first timeout of the game.
The Hawkeyes lined up again to attempt the conversion, but Iowa coach Kirk Ferentz called his first timeout.
After reconsidering the decision, Iowa punted. Boston Everitt’s kick traveled 42 yards and came to rest at Michigan’s three-yard line.
Bryce Underwood took the direct snap and gained seven yards up the middle, setting up second-and-three.
Underwood kept the ball on a quarterback read and gained three yards along the left sideline to move the chains.
With a fresh set of downs, Underwood lined up in the shotgun and connected with tight end Hogan Hansen for an eight-yard gain.
Running back Jordan Marshall then rushed for five yards before Underwood ran the read option and flipped the ball to Marshall for a three-yard gain down the right sideline.
Facing second-and-seven, Underwood handed the ball to Savion Hiter , who gained four yards.
On third-and-three, Michigan was called for its first penalty of the game when JJ Buchanan was flagged for a false start.
Facing third-and-8 after the penalty, Underwood scrambled for 8 yards, but Brady Norton was called for holding, pushing Michigan back to third-and-18.
On third-and-18, Underwood found a cutting Salesi Moa , but Moa dropped the pass.
Michigan was forced to punt, with Cameron Brown sending the ball to the 40-yard line, where Evan James fielded it with 6:42 remaining in the first quarter.
Moulton rushed up the left sideline for a three-yard gain before Rod Moore made the tackle.
On second down, Brown threw an incomplete pass to Tony Diaz, setting up a second-and-seven.
Brown threw another pass to Diaz, but Smith Snowden broke it up, setting up a punt that downed the ball at Michigan’s 11-yard line.
With 5:56 remaining in the quarter, Underwood found Andrew Marsh on a stick route, and Marsh turned upfield for a 27-yard catch-and-run.
Hiter then ran a jet sweep for 7 yards up the left side.
Underwood followed with a well-placed pass to Marsh along the right sideline.
Marsh made a contested shoulder catch for a 21-yard gain. The play was reviewed and upheld, with the ball moved to Iowa’s 35-yard line after Marsh was ruled to have kept his toes in bounds.
Underwood handed the ball to Hiter for 2 yards before tight end Jalen Hoffman caught a 3-yard pass.
Facing third-and-five, Underwood scrambled left and found Buchanan, who turned the catch into a 13-yard gain while dragging several defenders.
Marshall took a direct snap from the wildcat formation and gained three yards before Underwood threw a fade toward Marsh near the goal line.
On third-and-seven, Underwood scrambled to his right and found Buchanan on the right side of the end zone for an 18-yard touchdown.
Michigan was flagged for a false start on the extra-point attempt, moving the Wolverines back five yards.
Trey Butowski then converted the extra point to cap a nine-play, 89-yard drive that took 3:58.
Michigan took a 7-0 lead with 1:58 remaining in the quarter.
Baggett kicked the ball off 64 yards down to Iowa’s one-yard line, but Jackson made a house call as he returned the ball 99 yards.
Kicker Caden Buhr kicked the extra point to tie the game at 7-7 as the crowd went silent.
Running back Bryson Kuzdzal returned the kickoff 17 yards to the Wolverines’ 18-yard line.
Underwood kept the rock and gained two yards before finding Buchanan for a 22-yard catch-and-run.
With a new set of downs, Hiter took the read option and gained four yards to end the first quarter.
Michigan ended the quarter with 147 total yards, with 107 on the arm of Underwood and 40 on the ground.
The Wolverines’ defense held Iowa to 36 total yards, but the game was tied 7-7 as Michigan drove.
Michigan lined up in the wildcat. Marshall took the snap and handed it to Underwood on the jet sweep, who threw the pass to Marsh for an 11-yard gain.
Marsh was hit late out of bounds, giving Michigan 15 yards.
Underwood ran the keeper for a two-yard gain before Marshall missed the inside cut and stayed outside for a three-yard gain.
Facing third down and five, Underwood threw a wobbler to Marsh, but it fell incomplete as cornerback Jaylen Watson drilled him.
Butkowski drilled a field goal from 41 yards out to cap off an eight-play, 59-yard drive in 3:43 to take a 10-7 lead.
Xavier Williams returned the ball 29 yards and got hit, fumbling it as Michigan recovered, but the play was overturned because the ground caused the fumble.
With the ball on the 45-yard line, Moulton rushed left for four yards; Jyaire Hill made the tackle.
Moulton gained six yards on the next play up the gut.
With a fresh set of downs, Williams got stopped in the backfield for a loss of one.

articles.title_zh: Jon Watts Is Our ‘Star Wars: Episode X’ Director
articles.content_orig:
Even as Lucasfilm is deep in post-production on its next Star Wars movie, Star Wars: Starfighter , the next phase of a potential new Skywalker Saga is coming into focus.
Jon Watts , the director behind a trio of Tom Holland Spider-Man movies, is now attached to direct the first installment of the Simon Kinberg -penned trilogy. It is a return to the franchise for Watts, who previously co-created Star Wars series Skeleton Crew in 2024.
Kinberg has been working on writing a mystery trilogy since late 2024. The project is intended to act as the next chapter in what is referred to as the Skywalker Saga, the stories featuring the multi-generations of the Luke Skywalker family. The previous movies have been Episodes I through IX . The next one would be Episode X . Rey Skywalker, the Jedi played by Daisy Ridley in last trilogy released from 2015 and 2019, would appear in some capacity in the new trilogy.
Sources say the project is still in development and has not yet been greenlit by parent company Disney , although it seems to be project the furthest along the development track after Starfighter .
Starfighter is being directed by Shawn Levy and stars Ryan Gosling. The movie is expected to hit theatres May 27, 2027, coinciding with the 50th anniversary of Star Wars .
Watts is seen as a reliable choice for the franchise, which has occasionally, and would say famously, struggled with directors. After directing the indie thriller Cop Car , Watts was chosen by Marvel to helm the relaunch of the Spider-Man movies. The Tom Holland-starring movies, which included 2017’s Homecoming , 2019’s Far From Home , and 2021’s No Way Home , became progressively bigger productions and bigger hits at the box office. Watts proved he could navigate the complexities of massive big-budget productions.
His post- Spider-Man work included the George Clooney-Brad Pitt-starring Wolfs , the high-profile misfire from Apple that upended its theatrical release and curiously announced a sequel that was never going to be made.
Watts co-created and co-wrote Skeleton Crew , the well-regarded but unfortunately not greatly seen series that starred Jude Law and brought an Amblin vibe to the Star Wars universe. Watts directed two episodes of the show, which also had a starry assemblage of helmers that included David Lowery, Lee Isaac Chung, Jake Schreier, Bryce Dallas Howard, and the Daniels.
Knight Edge Media broke the news of Watts’ involvement.

articles.title_orig: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’
articles.title_zh: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’
articles.content_orig:
“ Godzilla Minus Zero” blew the roof off Alice Tully Hall during its rapturous world premiere screening at the New York Film Festival . The long-awaited sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” earned rave first reactions from the press earlier in the day, and that adoration rolled right into the world premiere. The movie was met with multiple mid-screening applauses as the crowd went wild for all the kaiju mayhem on screen.
Ahead of its debut later this year, “ Godzilla Minus Zero ” has been rated R for “violent content/bloody images,” making it the first entry in the 72-year-old franchise to receive an R-rating. Director Takashi Yamazaki , returning to helm the sequel after 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One” became a roaring success, says securing the rating was “essential to the film.” “Logically, as a studio — and even as a director — you want as many people from the general public to be able to see your film,” Yamazaki told Variety at the premiere Saturday afternoon. “So, an R-rating might seem like a barrier to entry, and conversations about, ‘Hey, could we have not gotten this down to PG-13?’ of course are going to happen. In spite of that, though, there were certain scenes that, for me as a director, were so essential to the film. Censoring it or cutting it was just not an option for me.”
Under MPA guidelines, viewers under 17 cannot attend an R-rated film without a parent or guardian, a restriction that has traditionally made the rating a commercial deterrent for studios releasing big-budget, four-quadrant films. That stigma has faded over the past decade, starting with the blockbuster success of 2016’s “Deadpool” ($782 million). In 2019, “Joker” ($1.07 billion) became the first R-rated film to cross the $1 billion threshold. That record was later broken by 2024’s “Deadpool & Wolverine” ($1.33 billion) — and more recently — 2026’s “The Odyssey” ($1.72 billion), which currently stands as the 17th highest-grossing film of all time worldwide.
“I think the R-rating, at one point, carried almost a negative connotation,” Yamazaki explained. “In more modern films, it actually creates a sort of expectation and excitement of, ‘Okay, well, they’re not censoring anything. The director and the cast’s voice is there, as is.’ So it is very encouraging to see other films who have preceded us that have already found a lot of success with the R-rating at the box office. Hopefully, we can continue that trend with ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.’”
Inside the world premiere screening, New York Film Festival director Dennis Lim acknowledged that the Godzilla franchise might not be the first thing people think of playing at a major film festival. And yet, “We thought it was about time to bring a giant monster movie here.”
Yamazaki took the stage to thunderous applause from the audience both before and after the screening, where he asked the crowd not to spoil any of the sequel’s many surprises on social media.
“You are the first to see this film,” the filmmaker said. “There are a lot of ‘Godzilla’ fans around the world, so let’s work together and do not do any spoilers. No spoilers, please! I am trusting all of you guys.”
Yamazaki also had the audience laughing while explaining how he never intended to create a sequel to “Godzilla Minus One.” Executives at Toho immediately started asking him about a follow-up movie once they saw the first cut of “Minus One,” a thought that made Yamazaki instantly nervous. It wasn’t until the movie opened in theaters and started to be celebrated around the world by audiences that the director realized a sequel would be a viable option.
“Toho executives are here,” the director said. “With your reactions tonight I hope they don’t offer a third movie.”

articles.title_zh: Godzilla Minus Zero review: R-rated sequel follows in the first's cavernous footsteps
articles.content_orig:
New York film festival: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
E ven by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago. Godzilla Minus One , the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in a series of Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn’t just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Now. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and the Toho -made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. Arguably the artsiest, brainiest of the major fall fests is playing unexpected host to a truly spectacular monster battle royale, packaged alongside some of the same thoughtful historical context that informed the previous film.
Writer, director and VFX maestro Takashi Yamazaki returns for the sequel, bringing his lead characters back with him. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience with Godzilla to overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to “zero”, hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to “minus one”. Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn’t seen directly in trailers, this isn’t a spoiler; he’s featured from the very first scene of the film.)
Ghidorah’s appearance obviously sends off alarms in the disaster-response agency that now employs Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), also from the previous film. Noda is joined by Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist who introduces less artillery-heavy defense mechanisms for this new threat. Of course, there is a natural Ghidorah deterrent last seen disintegrating into the sea but known for his adaptability – if only the big guy could be called upon and steered in the right direction.
In the older Godzilla films, Ghidorah-Godzilla battles can sometimes make whatever humans who might fit into the picture seem all the more insignificant; the monsters are so fearsome and, in their way, charismatic, that they level anything else in their way. In the tradition of its emotionally involving predecessor, Godzilla Minus Zero grapples more directly with humans’ attempts to assert some control over forces that initially seem impossible to harness. It’s no accident that one of its new heroes attempts to predict the weather – and has faced natural disasters despite her accurate predictions. The characters wield technology that is more science-fictionally advanced than in the previous movie while still relying on a sense of impromptu can-do scrappiness and determination to protect their country. With decreased puny-human helplessness comes greater dangers and new dilemmas.
The film’s version of the US military, for example, is willing to provide planes but not troops to aid in the fight, which is partially how Kōichi and Noriko are drawn back into the conflict despite the pleading of young Akiko. The partners’ skill sets make them valuable assets, perpetuating some of the previous film’s questions about what kinds of sacrifices might be expected or required when sending citizens into the thick of battle. There’s also an element of body horror used intriguingly, but perhaps not to its fullest potential, given the shiver of anticipation that shoots through the audience when it’s introduced.
There’s some value in sidestepping expectations; Yamazaki mentioned at a NYFF press conference that he sought to avoid conforming to any fan guesswork about how various kaiju business in a sequel to Minus One might proceed. True to his word, the movie seems determined to stay true to the human melodrama that proved so surprisingly effective in the previous film, rather than going into all-out monsters-attack mode. That approach works well for the film’s new characters as well as for Noda (Yoshioka is especially good reprising the role), but sometimes falters when it comes to the family-soap parts of the story, which manage to be both more tearful (onscreen) and less (in the audience, though obviously some mileage will vary). The restrained relationship between Kōichi and Noriko made sense last time; in a movie two years later, their nominally romantic partnership seems weirdly glum, even anti-sexual, in a state of co-parenting stasis. There’s little sense of time’s passage for this makeshift family.
That’s not to say that the monster-attack stuff falls by the wayside in favor of the humans. In fact, the movie’s extended climax features some of the most majestic CG monster action put to film; if the fun American MonsterVerse series tends toward pro-wrestling kaiju, Godzilla Minus Zero cross-breeds its fight-to-the-death grappling with disaster-movie scope and horror-movie teeth. Yet it also doesn’t go in for the overkill; like its predecessor, the movie favors quality of visual effects over quantity. Little-yet-huge details like Ghidorah’s lightning-like attack beams have a jagged beauty that makes them both cooler and scarier than so many obligatory effects-movie laser shows.
It’s a fittingly judicious use of computers, given that the world of Godzilla Minus Zero often appears perched on the verge of a post-war technology boom, and on the precipice of the further global disasters that could be invited by the collision of humankind’s supposed innovations and unknowable forces of nature. (Minus One came out the same year as Oppenheimer; was this one, like Nolan’s The Odyssey, conceived in its wake?) If Yamazaki’s previous Godzilla movie ultimately allowed crowd-pleasing thrills to punch through its mid-century anxieties, this one lands a bit more ambiguously. Maybe that’s why the melodrama stuff isn’t quite so satisfying this time around; attentive as the movie is to its human cast, it’s increasingly clear that we’re living in a world of monsters.
Godzilla Minus Zero is screening at the New York film festival and will be released in Australia on 5 November and in the US and the UK on 6 November
